feed.title: Networking & Sysadmin — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: A Cartoon Intro to DNS over HTTPS
entry.content:
A Mozilla article that uses cartoons to explain why DNS is a privacy problem and how DoH changes it. Unlike protocol specs it assumes no background and quickly shows what the DoH debate is about.

https://hacks.mozilla.org/2018/05/a-cartoon-intro-to-dns-over-https/

entry.title: Awesome eBPF (qmonnet)
entry.content:
A list of eBPF projects, articles and tools, with compilers, tracing and networking (XDP) under separate headings. Unlike the other eBPF list already in the directory it is still being updated, and is kept by someone who writes eBPF documentation.

https://github.com/qmonnet/awesome-ebpf

entry.title: Bridgy Fed
entry.content:
A service that bridges websites, the fediverse (Mastodon etc.) and Bluesky/AT Protocol so accounts can follow and reply across networks. Unlike single-network clients, it translates between the protocols themselves.

https://fed.brid.gy

entry.title: ciphersuite.info
entry.content:
A reference site that lists every TLS cipher suite searchably, with IANA and OpenSSL names, a security rating (secure/weak/insecure) and protocol-version support. For when you meet a suite name and want to know what it means and whether to allow it. Unlike the raw IANA registry, it gives each suite a readable security rating.

https://ciphersuite.info/

entry.title: curl
entry.content:
The site for the standard command-line tool for transferring data with URLs and for the libcurl library; it has the manual, a protocol list and the free book "Everything curl". With "copy as cURL" in browser dev tools it is the basic way to debug an API call. It makes a request repeatable from the command line, instead of living only in browser dev tools.

https://curl.se/

entry.title: DKIM Validator
entry.content:
Send a test email to the temporary address it gives you and it reports SPF, DKIM and SpamAssassin scores. Instead of checking records in isolation, it tests a real message end to end.

https://dkimvalidator.com/

entry.title: DNSlytics
entry.content:
A research site showing DNS records, sites sharing an IP, mail/whois data and history for a domain, IP or autonomous-system number. Unlike ViewDNS's one-shot queries it links a domain to its hosting and ASN relationships.

https://dnslytics.com/

entry.title: DNSSEC Debugger
entry.content:
Verisign's tool that validates a domain's DNSSEC chain of trust from the root down and shows where it breaks. Unlike general DNS checkers it concentrates on the signature chain alone.

https://dnssec-debugger.verisignlabs.com/

entry.title: IntoDNS
entry.content:
A quick checker for a domain's DNS and mail (MX) setup that lists errors and warnings point by point. Less thorough than Zonemaster, but the result sits on one readable page.

https://intodns.com/

entry.title: Is BGP safe yet?
entry.content:
A Cloudflare page that tests from your browser whether your ISP filters invalid BGP routes (RPKI). It turns an abstract topic, routing security, into a one-click result. Unlike the technical RPKI documentation, it gives you the answer in one click from your browser.

https://isbgpsafeyet.com/

entry.title: MultiRBL
entry.content:
Looks up an IP or domain in hundreds of DNS blocklists (RBLs) at once. Shows which list is behind a mail server being rejected, and also checks forward and reverse DNS consistency. Rather than checking one blocklist, it queries hundreds of RBLs at once.

https://multirbl.valli.org/

entry.title: MxToolbox SuperTool
entry.content:
An email and DNS diagnostic that runs MX, DNS, blacklist, SPF, DMARC, ping and port lookups from a single box. A common first stop for mail delivery problems, replacing several single-purpose checkers. Unlike single-purpose checkers, it runs MX, SPF, DMARC and blacklist lookups from one box.

https://mxtoolbox.com/SuperTool.aspx

entry.title: nip.io
entry.content:
A wildcard DNS service that resolves names like 10.0.0.1.nip.io to the IP embedded in them, so you can reach a local or test server by hostname without editing the hosts file. No setup or sign-up. Instead of editing /etc/hosts, it embeds the address in the name itself.

https://nip.io/

entry.title: OpenInfraMap
entry.content:
A map rendering power lines, plants, oil/gas pipelines and telecom infrastructure from OpenStreetMap data. Unlike general maps, it has infrastructure-specific layers with voltage and capacity detail.

https://openinframap.org

entry.title: OpenSSL
entry.content:
The official site of the TLS/SSL and general-purpose cryptography library and the openssl command-line tool; command manuals, release notes and library API docs live here. The basic reference for generating certificates, converting keys and inspecting a handshake against a server. It is a library as well as a command tool, so it covers more than single-purpose certificate utilities.

https://www.openssl.org/

entry.title: OpenSSL Certificate Authority
entry.content:
A step-by-step guide to building a root and intermediate certificate authority with OpenSSL, signing certificates and publishing revocation lists. Unlike ready-made CA software it shows the file layout and configuration by hand, so you see how a PKI works.

https://jamielinux.com/docs/openssl-certificate-authority/

entry.title: RIPE Atlas
entry.content:
RIPE NCC's network of thousands of small probes that run ping, traceroute and DNS measurements from around the world. It lets you see a target from other countries and operators rather than your own connection, which helps diagnose reachability problems.

https://atlas.ripe.net/

entry.title: Scapy
entry.content:
An interactive Python library for forging, sending, capturing and decoding packets; the site hosts docs and examples. Unlike Wireshark you build and mutate packets in code, and unlike Nmap you write your own protocol tests rather than using canned scans.

https://scapy.net/

entry.title: Submarine Cable Map
entry.content:
TeleGeography's interactive map of the world's submarine internet cables, landing points and owners. Unlike generic network maps it makes the physical backbone of the internet traceable cable by cable.

https://www.submarinecablemap.com/

entry.title: ViewDNS.info
entry.content:
A toolbox of dozens of DNS and domain queries in one place: reverse IP lookup, DNS history, whois, a port scanner, domain-to-IP mapping. Each query is a small separate tool and no sign-up is needed.

https://viewdns.info/

entry.title: Zonemaster
entry.content:
A checker that runs a domain's DNS setup (delegation, SOA, DNSSEC, nameserver consistency) through dozens of tests; the open-source engine of the Swedish registry. Unlike tools that query one record, it reports on the whole zone against a standard test suite.

https://zonemaster.se/en/

entry.title: goshs
entry.content:
A single-binary file server written in Go, supporting HTTP, WebDAV, FTP/SFTP, SMB and more. Unlike python -m http.server it adds uploads, authentication and more protocols; its red-team features mean you should use it only on systems you own.

https://github.com/goshs-labs/goshs

entry.title: lazyssh
entry.content:
A terminal UI that lists the hosts in your SSH config and connects to them (Go). Unlike editing ~/.ssh/config by hand and remembering names it gives a searchable list.

https://github.com/Adembc/lazyssh

entry.title: mactop
entry.content:
A terminal monitor for Apple Silicon showing CPU, GPU and power use. Unlike htop it reads Apple-specific sensors (power, GPU, neural engine).

https://github.com/metaspartan/mactop

entry.title: Sniffnet
entry.content:
A cross-platform app that shows network traffic in a friendly interface (Rust). Unlike Wireshark it favours a readable overview over packet-level detail.

https://github.com/GyulyVGC/sniffnet

entry.title: Awesome Arch
entry.content:
A list of Arch Linux–based distributions and projects. Unlike the Arch Wiki, it collects not documentation but the distributions derived from Arch and their tools, side by side.

https://github.com/PandaFoss/Awesome-Arch

entry.title: Awesome eBPF
entry.content:
A resource list for eBPF, which runs safe programs inside the kernel. Unlike writing a kernel module, the program must first pass the verifier, so it runs without the risk of crashing the kernel.

https://github.com/zoidbergwill/awesome-ebpf

entry.title: Awesome GNOME
entry.content:
A list of apps and extensions for the GNOME desktop environment. Unlike the KDE list, it covers GTK/libadwaita apps that follow GNOME’s interface guidelines, plus shell extensions.

https://github.com/Kazhnuz/awesome-gnome

entry.title: Awesome IPFS
entry.content:
A list of tools and projects for IPFS, the decentralised file protocol. Unlike HTTP, it addresses a file by the hash of its content (CID) rather than by the server that holds it.

https://github.com/ipfs/awesome-ipfs

entry.title: Awesome KDE
entry.content:
A list of apps and resources for the KDE desktop environment. Unlike the GNOME list, it focuses on Qt-based KDE apps and Plasma customisation.

https://github.com/francoism90/awesome-kde

entry.title: Awesome Scapy
entry.content:
A list of tools and examples for Scapy, the Python packet-manipulation library. Unlike general network lists it centres on crafting and sending packets by hand.

https://github.com/secdev/awesome-scapy

entry.title: Awesome Windows
entry.content:
A list of recommended apps and tools for the Windows desktop. Unlike the Microsoft Store it is curated and puts free and open-source options first.

https://github.com/0pandadev/awesome-windows

entry.title: Comcast
entry.content:
Injects network latency and packet loss to test how software copes under bad conditions. Instead of hand-writing tc/netem and iptables commands, it produces the same effect with one command.

https://github.com/tylertreat/Comcast

entry.title: Lokinet
entry.content:
A decentralised, IP-based onion-routing network that anonymises traffic across staked nodes. Unlike Tor it carries any IP protocol, not just web: a full overlay network on top of onion routing rather than a single application.

https://lokinet.org/

entry.title: Check Point Eğitim
entry.content:
The CCSA and CCSE certifications. What differs from other firewall vendors is that Check Point’s management architecture is its own body of knowledge — centralised policy management sits at the centre of the training.

https://training-certifications.checkpoint.com/

entry.title: Cisco Sertifikasyon
entry.content:
The networking certification programme from CCNA to CCIE. Unlike vendor-neutral certificates it is specific to Cisco equipment; even so, CCNA is widely treated as a solid networking fundamentals curriculum regardless of vendor.

https://www.cisco.com/site/us/en/learn/training-certifications/

entry.title: Fortinet Training Institute
entry.content:
The NSE programme and security training. Against other vendor programmes most of it has been made free — the broadest no-cost resource for firewall and network security fundamentals.

https://training.fortinet.com/

entry.title: Juniper Sertifikasyon
entry.content:
Junos-based networking certifications. Against Cisco’s programme the entry-level exams have long been offered free and the training material is open — the no-cost route into networking.

https://www.juniper.net/us/en/training/certification/

entry.title: Linux Professional Institute
entry.content:
Distribution-neutral Linux certifications (LPIC-1, LPIC-2). Against Red Hat’s programme it is not tied to one distribution — this is the certificate that still applies if you run Debian, SUSE or Arch.

https://www.lpi.org/

entry.title: Palo Alto Networks Eğitim
entry.content:
PCNSA and PCNSE certifications with firewall and cloud security training. Against Fortinet it targets the upper enterprise segment — the certificate pays off directly at organisations running those products.

https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/services/education
